utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. I would just like to inform you that my client is still not feeling well, and, as you can see, he is not present in the courtroom, but we can continue without him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation, and we notice that he was not feeling well yesterday afternoon. We only wish him a speedy recovery. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Before we continue on, let me go back to a couple of thoughts from yesterday, please. During the time that you served in the vicinity of Gornji Vakuf, what was your position or rank or function at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a rank. I commanded a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A platoon. So did you have any sort of functional -- if you didn't wear a particular insignia, did you have a functional rank of platoon commander, something -- second lieutenant, any such terminology used in connection with your military service at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wore the HVO insignia, and there were also insignia for platoon commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you wear that insignia, for a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with your military service and all of the background that we talked about yesterday, just one other thing that I didn't ask. Have you ever attended a military academy or professional military school?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never attended a military academy. I served my compulsory military service in the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps, against my better judgement - I'm not sure - I'm going to ask you the next question, sir, it has nothing to do with what's written in your report and I do not want to get into the same difficulty, hopefully, that we had at the end of the day yesterday. So apart from what's in your report, let me simply ask you this question: In your role as an historian and in your work that you have done, was Franjo Tudjman obsessed with the division of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, as regards this obsession, if I remember it well, yesterday afternoon issued a false statement, saying that I was the one who mentioned that word in my report. I read the report three times again, and I didn't find it. Secondly, I am a historian. I'm not the one who knows, but the one who searches for the truth. So far, I haven't found any evidence for such an allegation. The allegation about Franjo Tudjman being obsessed with the division of Bosnia has been served to the general public for years. This allegation comes from certain circles in Croatia, but also in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what circles in Croatia does it come from?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These circles are those around the former magazine Erasmus, and they can mostly be linked with sociology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In any event, sir, the policy, again, going back to your report, on page 21, is it correct that the policy of the Republic of Croatia was based on a situation where the Bosnian Croat leadership, or at least the HDZ/HVO leadership, wanted to unify the Croatian parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina into a unified Croatian state, that is, as part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please indicate the footnote where I can find this part in my report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, there's a fairly long stretch on page 21 in the English version without a footnote, but it occurs between footnote 161 and footnote 162. In the English version, it begins -- it is the first sentence of the third paragraph starting on page 21. And let me just read it to you, with the translation -- help of the translators: "The politics of RH, the Republic of Croatia, towards BH, as a state, in which one of the constitutional nations are also the Croats, obviously had a desire for unification into an integral Croatian state. That is indisputable." That's your position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it. This report was written on the 12th of July, 2002. That's when it was completed. And I believe that it was on the same day that I handed it over to Mr. Par. This is not my usual practice. I usually leave my papers to rest for a month or so. I leave them aside, and then I go back to them. I revisit my papers to find the possible mistakes. When I was rereading it some 15 days ago, I crossed some things out; in some places I found things not easy to understand; and I also found some mistakes, some errors. One of these errors is as follows: Instead of "RH" here, I would put "Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina," and the rest of this passage I wouldn't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So putting aside for the moment the broader matters that you've raised, you agree, then, with the sentence I read you, with the suggested modification that instead of saying, "the politics of RH," you would say, "the politics of the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think, and I have to express my reservations here, with a little hedging, I can say that historians very often assume things, but this is clearly denoted. This opinion of mine is mostly based on my personal contacts. I did not meet more than two Croats from Bosnia who were not geared towards Zagreb, who did not turn their eyes towards Zagreb. In addition to that, I quoted here a document from December 1991, and I have to admit that I never saw that document. The only place I came across this document is Bosniak historiography. There are people who think that this document is not authentic. To my mind, it is inconceivable for a professional historian, such as Smail Cekic, who mentioned it first, would reduce himself down to that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is visible from this document -- please allow me to finish, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am going to cut you off, because my time, sir, is going to be limited, and I'm sure counsel will remind me of that. And what you're saying now is not responsive to the question that I asked you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to answer, if I may, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness should be allowed to answer; otherwise we will arrive at misunderstandings. In addition to that, my witness has been interrupted in mid-sentence. I think he should be allowed to finish that sentence at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think, you know, the Prosecution put a very simple question: Do I understand you correctly? The witness said yes. I think -- then he gave some explanations. We get most of the answers in the transcript already. We have to move on. Mr. Scott, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true, based on all this, based on your report and what you said just now, that in fact the HDZ and the HVO did more or less, perhaps not identical things, but more or less the same thing as you say that the Bosnian Serbs and the SDS did, just as they wanted a Greater Serbia connected to Belgrade, the HDZ and the HVO wanted a greater Croatia connected to Zagreb? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you are putting the sign of equality between Serbs and Croats, and this brings me back to the first part of my testimony. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was created as a defence organisation. When it became clear that the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and its president, Mr. Izetbegovic, were not interested in anything but the destiny of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me go back to my question, sir. Perhaps if you'll answer this question. Isn't it true that the HDZ and the HVO had and carried out a desire to create a greater Croatia connected to Zagreb, in a similar way that the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, wished to create a Greater Serbia connected to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not have similar intentions. They didn't have the intention to do what the Serbs do, because what the Serbs did is unparalleled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, how is it different, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, there is a problem, in addition to the document that I have just mentioned, I did not come across any other documents, and I am an historian who uses documents rather than prejudices. I have not seen documents indicating that somebody from the Croatian Defence Council, or from the HDZ, spoke about the time of unification with the Republic of Croatia. Because of the policy pursued by the international community, which persistently divided Bosnia, they didn't need to do that. That is my opinion. As regards your question, sir, it is very clear how Republika Srpska came about to be after ethnical cleansing, after an aggressive war with concentration camps, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, sir, the difference, what you're telling us, if I hear you, and building on what you told the Judges yesterday, you say there were differences between what the HVO did and what the Serbs did. You're saying it was a matter of degree. They did similar things, but your contention that the HVO wasn't as bad as the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a very liberal interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, didn't --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO never denied or never fought against being an integral part of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Even when HVO was always within that framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't think, sir, that in the document we looked at yesterday, where Mate Boban said that the legal armed forces of the nation admitted to the United Nations, when Mr. Boban said those were illegal forces on the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna, you don't think that was an attack on Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have just mentioned the United Nations. Are you referring to something that you call the legal authorities or the legal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... exhibit yesterday, and if Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. necessary we'll pull it out again. I showed it to you, dated approximately the 10th of April, 1992. And when Mr. Boban declared that the HVO armed forces were the only legal forces on the territory of what was claimed of the so-called Herceg-Bosna, and that all other forces, including those of Bosnia and Herzegovina, were illegal; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a correct statement. Can you please give me an example illustrating the situation when the HVO chased out from, so to say, their territory, the, so to say, legal forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know how the 4th Corps of the BH army came to be? It originated from the HVO. So you should make a distinction between what it says on the paper and what really happened. We are here talking about a conflict between two methodologies, one very superficial, belonging to you, that I would illustrate in the following way: Based -- using this microphone, you are trying to describe the desk in front of you. I'm looking at the historical truth, not speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, the HDZ, or the Bosnian Croat declaration -- excuse me - the HDZ declaration establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, on the 18th of November, 1991, actually preceded the similar Serb declaration, didn't it, the Serb declaration that you said started the war, which was not until the 21st of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that sometime in 1991, mid-1991, the Serbs in Krajina organised joint manoeuvres of the army, more specifically, it was Mile Martic and Bosanski Petrovac. I believe that they issued a joint resolution on unification that was repeated at least twice. After that, Mr. Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the document that you cite in your report on page 6, it was the Bosnian Serb decision dated the 21st of December, 1991, titled "constituting the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat? I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll continue on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to please show the witness Exhibit IAC 2 [Realtime transcript read in error"IHC"]. Just so the record -- Mr. Poriouvaev has indicated that the transcript says "IHC," and it's "IAC." If you could place that on the ELMO, perhaps give -- the witness may wish to look at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a declaration of the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community, dated the 12th of November, 1991, over the name of Mate Boban, for the Herzegovina community, and Dario Kordic for the Travnik or Central Bosnia community. Have you seen this document before and have you considered it in stating any of the opinions or conclusions in your report or things that you've testified to the Chamber here in the last couple of days?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You obviously haven't read my paper. I have quoted this document in it. I have quoted it from Mr. Cekic's book. A little while ago I expressed my reservations about that book. This is the first time I actually see this document. It is a copy of the document. Whether this copy is authentic or not, I really wouldn't be able to say. But in this document there is this sentence about our long dream about a unified Croatia, and this is the sentence that I have quoted in my paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In addition to that, sir, before we get to that, in the paragraph -- the paragraph numbered 1, after "conclusions," does it not talk about -- well, does it not say this: "The Croatian regional community and the Travnik regional community remain of the opinion stated in the conclusions adopted at earlier meetings, that the Croatian people of this region, and all Bosnia and Herzegovina, still support the unanimously accepted orientation and conclusions adopted in agreements with president Franjo Tudjman on 13th and 20th June 1991 in Zagreb." And it then goes on to talk about meetings on the 15th of October, the 22nd of October, and on this occasion it says the 12th of November, 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe your interpretation to be correct, and I know that you will give me the minutes of these two meetings as your next exhibits. This looks as if it had been written for your purpose, to serve your purpose. Can I get these minutes, please? Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Can I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you listen to my questions, not make speeches, it will assist us. You said just now this was a document that you had quoted in your report, sir, so don't indicate that I had made it for my own purposes. Now, directing your attention to that -- end of that same paragraph, did the report not say, simply to confirm if this is in your report, that "The Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina must finally embrace a determined and active policy which will realise our eternal dream, a common Croatian state"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may not fully understand why the witness is interrupted and not being allowed to explain, why is the Prosecutor twisting the words of this witness. The witness was very clear when he said that he came across the document in the book authored by a Bosniak author and that he never saw it before and that he doubts its authenticity. Why does then my learned friend continue asking questions about this document after such clear answers given by my witness? I've been following the transcript, and I believe that the answers by my witness have been very clear. In addition to that, Your Honour, I don't want to say anything in order to avoid Her Honour Clark's warnings, but we've had people here who allegedly signed this document, and you know their answers about this document, and I really don't know where all this is leading to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we found a very surprise from the testimony of this witness. Since he already used a certain paragraph of this declaration, he has no right to challenge the authority, the authenticity of this document at all. That's very strange, you know. Well, I'm not arguing with you. The second issue is that it seems to me - well, I think as well as you - that we are the laymen to history as a science. I think two interpretations of the history: One is the evidence, hard evidence, whatever that has been happened. The other interpretation of history is the historian's interpretation of history, the historian's opinions, comments, of the history. Here we have a report. It seems to us it is not only the hard evidence itself but also the opinion, the comments, the interpretation of the author himself. The Prosecutor is trying to tell us what is the hard evidence, what has been already happened, and what is the interpretation, his concept of this witness. I think it's quite normal. That's normal procedures. What's the problem with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to do here, because I hear answers of one kind, and all of you hear answers of another kind. And I quite understand what the witness is saying. Like also yesterday the problem with obsession. Well, if that is, then let's have this paper translated once again by translators of this Tribunal. He says that he quoted this text from a book of a Bosniak author and that is what he quoted. And he says he never laid eyes on it and questions its authenticity. But he saw this text in a book by a Bosniak author. I don't know what is unclear here, because obviously we are talking at cross-purposes and we do not understand one another, and I do not think that this testimony is of any value. Because I hear one thing and everybody else hears something else. This is just too dangerous, because I hear him speak in the original, in Croatian, and I understand his paper written in Croatian. I also understand the Croatian answers, the answers in Croatian that the witness is giving, and that the witness denies the authenticity of this document because it was found in the Bosnian historiography by a Bosniak author and today -- and he is explaining it to us today. Your Honours, I am completely perplexed. I really don't know what to do now, because incomprehension is obviously linguistic or I don't know what, or perhaps somebody doesn't know how to convey the spirit of the language either in this translation or perhaps in interpretation. I don't know, because my English is not so good. I understand, and I hear what the witness is saying. So allow him to give his explanations, because these are very important things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for yesterday afternoon's sentence, the obsession issues, we ask the interpretation for three times. At least the interpreters translated in this courtroom for at least three times. We don't see any significant differences with the translation of this report. So I don't believe it's a question of translation. I think it's a question of we are talking cross-purpose. I have already said that we have to know what is the hard evidence, what is the facts, what has already happened and what is the interpretation of these experts. That's the only purpose. Different historians have different interpretations towards the same hard evidence. Our job is to distinguish the two. So in this way, I think Mr. Scott's question is somehow on this line, so we will allow him to continue. Mr. Scott, would you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the statement that I read to you, that was the position of the Bosnian Croat leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct, leading to the creation of Herceg-Bosna, and that was to realise our eternal dream, a common Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what transpires from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown, please, P104 and P103. I'm going to take them numerically in opposite -- take 104 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the course of your work, you're familiar, are you not, with the declaration dated the 18th of November, 1991, declaring the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was published in the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as it says in Article 1, this declaration was to "establish Herceg-Bosna as a political, economic, and territorial whole." And there's another 104 -- 103 - excuse me - a better document for these purposes. But that's correct, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which? Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you may want to look, and when I pointed you to 104, I see now for this particular item, 103 is actually clearer in terms of the translation. Article 1 says: "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be founded as a political, cultural, economic, and territorial whole." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Article 3, they declared Mostar to be the seat of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with - excuse me - Exhibit P103, this has -- this particular version has been amended, and as it says here, on the 3rd of July, 1992, to add a little additional language, which is here called "reasons." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under "reasons," under the third paragraph under that, toward the end -- well, about halfway through the third paragraph under reasons, it talks about the unacceptability of a unitary model of state order in multi-ethnic societies. What was unacceptable about a unitary model of a multi-ethnic society?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a civil state: One man, one vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what's wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political force of a people is seen in the number -- of the size of the population, or rather, that is the view of the Muslim side, according to which they would have fared the best. If it had been done, and neither the Serbs nor the Croats agreed to that. As for the reasons for the establishment, I believe they are explained well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- sorry, sir. The translation -- I thought you were finished.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this was six days after the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the position of the HDZ at the time, the view or the working assumption, as I understand your paper, was that Bosnia-Herzegovina would not survive, was not going to survive, in any event, so it was a short step from here to becoming part of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really put it that way. You're again very free, very liberal when you quote my paper. And I'd like to read something to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at, on page 20, do you not say: "The Croatian politics towards Bosnia-Herzegovina obviously had a starting point in the assumption that Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot survive"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my view. However, as far as I know, that is Mr. Izetbegovic's view. In the footnote 31, you have his conversation with Mr. Tudgman after the elections, so that even Mr. Izetbegovic was -- understood quite well that Bosnia could not survive, as you can see today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's correct, sir, that --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Divided, split, by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You agree, sir, that Croatian politics toward BH obviously had a starting point in the assumption that BH cannot survive; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Croatian policies, perception was that Bosnia-Herzegovina could not survive as an integral whole, but once again we are faced with a problem of evidence. We have documents from 1991 which say one thing, and the day before yesterday I showed you at least 15 documents testifying to something else, and these -- they also have the seal, the category, the reference number, and one knows where they are kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say, shortly after that are in your report on page 20, "The views of Franjo Tudjman on Bosnia-Herzegovina were not a secret. He did not believe in its viability." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that sometime towards the end of 1991 Mr. Tudjman said something in this vein. He spoke openly. It was his opinion that it could not survive. You can find it in the press dating to December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for Croats, you say also on page 20, you say, "for Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was a war for emancipation with a wish to integrate with the parent country." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I already explained it at the beginning of this set. I said that it was my view on the basis of my personal insights, and this is again an interesting question which is erased today: Why don't the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina see that state as their state? Perhaps because during the communism they were not treated in line with the constitution and laws that you so faithfully obey. But I didn't say ever that they wanted it. I do not think that there is a single document with such a clear view, not even in the forgery yesterday which you attempted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Interpreter's correction. Not that they wanted it, but when they wanted to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for the documents of the 12th of November, it refers to two others, and it can be easily checked. You had access to the archive of the president of the republic in contrast with me. I suppose you have records of the meeting. Everything was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on page 21, you say that "By mid-1992 the political option, whose fundamental objective was to annex the Croatian ethnic parts to Croatia, had practically made most of their wishes come true." How had those wishes come true by mid-1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me where is that again, if you could give me a footnote?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is after footnote 161, in the first paragraph starting on the top of page 21 in the English version. You're talking about as early as mid-1992, and then in your next sentence you say, "At that time, the political option, whose fundamental objective was to annex the Croatian ethnic parts to Croatia had practically made most of their wishes come true." Now, what wishes had come true by mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I wrote this, it is indisputable that in the Croat Democratic Union, or rather the HVO, there was an option which was wholeheartedly for the unification with Croatia. By 1992, it had already accomplished its military goal, and you can find the best picture of it in a letter by Alija Izetbegovic, of which I only found a fragment of I believe the 5th of July, 1992, and Franjo Tudjman's answer, from which one can see that yes, the option is on the table, but he does not go along with it. So one thing were the wishes of the Croat and circumstances were another matter. I believe you have those letters. Unfortunately, I do not. All I have is Mr. Tudjman's reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is: How was it that by mid-1992 the fundamental objective of being annexed to Croatia had mostly come true?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the HVO had practically preserved a major part, militarily, and there was still some fighting in Posavina and around Jajce. And again I see here, I believe, that the option is -- well, let's say if we regionally singled it out, the Herzegovina option was slightly stronger, unlike some other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in connection with that part of your report that we were just looking at, that same paragraph, where you said, "As early as mid-1992, BH Croats managed (with the help from the Croatian army and Croatian politics) to canalise the conflict with the Serbs into two battlefields: Jajce and the Bosnian Posavina." So moving into the topic, sir, of the involvement of the Croatian army, you agree, do you not, that throughout most of 1992, the Croatian army played a significant role in Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1992, as I wrote here, was in a border areas quite strong, especially along the Neretva Prevlaka line, and it played a major role insofar as Bosnia-Herzegovina itself was concerned, because it practically prevented the extinction of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Secondly, it helped - and I mention it in a place - the analysis of how much of the army of Republika Srpska it tied up. And it also indirectly helped the Territorial Defence, subsequently the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina significantly. Sometime as of September, that is, end of August, from the area of the late operative zone. No. It was already operative zone north-west Herzegovina. And members of the Croatian army who were very few in number there were withdrawn. There were some of them in Posavina, until October 1992, and down on the southern front, around borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, most of the documents you showed us yesterday, the Defence exhibits -- or excuse me, on Tuesday - were from 1992, in terms of assistance being provided to the Muslims, and that was when the Croats and Muslims, during that time, were more or less fighting against the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. You can find them in 1993. The last one is of the 30th of March, 1993. And I believe that by mid-April the assistance from the Republic of Croatia stopped when the BH army started cleansing Croats from its territories in Konjic, in Jablanica, where they were symbolic as compared with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in connection with your -- the exhibit D2/78, that had to do specifically with the Tuzla area in eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was an area -- that was a particular situation where the Muslims and Croats fought together against the Serbs throughout the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My documents are not marked. Do you mean the document of the 2nd Corps of the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's right, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In that area there was no fighting between Croats and Muslims, never during the war, except that Muslims accounted for some 25 per cent of the HVO units there for the duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we need to, we can look at the map, but Tuzla is on the complete opposite side of the country as Mostar and Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tuzla is approximately below Bosnia and Posavina, in the northern part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as you said just a moment ago, and as you say in your report, whatever your contention is about the Croatian support to the Muslims, it ended by March, or at most early -- April, excuse me, April 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that after the middle of April, until about the middle of another April, or perhaps May 1994, that is, for a whole year, I did not see a single document of that nature. Only then the assistance was resumed, which covers the whole period of the Muslim/Croat war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell the Judges, please, in the terminology that was used by the Croatian army, perhaps also by the HVO, what was the southern front?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the southern front expression, and that is a part of the Split operative zone, which became independent sometime in April 1992, and existed as such until the end of the war against the Serbs. So that is until the end of 1995. In that area, we can say, from Ploce, that is, the Neretva mouth, in the Adriatic Sea, to Prevlaka, the border with Montenegro. That is the southern front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, perhaps we can save a little bit of time if there's no dispute about it, as reflected in Exhibit P123.2, Croatian army General Janko Bobetko was appointed by President Tudjman as commander of the southern front on the 10th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It is correct. I believe he published his document in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did General Bobetko continue to be the commander of the southern front throughout all of 1992 and 1993, or were there other persons in that position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, late, sometime around November 1992, that was when General Bobetko became the chief of the Main Staff of the Croatian army. I believe he was first replaced by Nojko Marinovic, and then Zivko Budimir, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Mr. Marinovic was he the commander of the southern front through, then, the balance of 1992 and all of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that Bobetko was until the end of 1992, almost, and Marinovic was then the commander of the 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army from Dubrovnik. And when Bobetko left that position, he took over the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. southern front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "he," Mr. Marinovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is who I mean, Mr. Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, sir, just so that we're clear for the record purposes: He continued to be the commander of the southern front, then, through all of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact. I don't know until when. He was wounded, but I believe that he was the commander throughout 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And moving forward, sir, there's no dispute, is there, that the HV was engaged in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in southern Herzegovina and in the area described yesterday as the Bosnian Posavina, during the spring and fall of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you say that on -- as early as the 7th of April, 1992, at page 10, that "the HV chief inspector asked the Croatian Minister of Defence to organise a group, approximately 1.200 soldiers, to go to Bosnia to fight against the Serbs." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're really doing something forceful to my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I believe I am simply reading it back to you. If you want to look at page 10 ...

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you like me to read this part to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir. Just answer my question. It's correct, isn't it, that the HV --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just the other way around, sir. It is not correct, Mr. Prosecutor, General Martin Spegelj asked from the Minister of Defence to allow for 1.200 men, mostly Muslims, to be sent out, and this is the document that you have got. And it is given in -- it was given during the first part of the day. You have it. Maybe it wouldn't be a bad idea for you to read my text. You keep repeating that you have read it, and you are constantly demonstrating the opposite by your actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Although yesterday you rejected my objection, I will repeat it again, just for the record, because this record will be read by people in the future. It is not going to be just for us in the courtroom. It will be the second instance court, the historians, or maybe just my son, who is also a lawyer. I object to all these questions when the Prosecutor repeats the direct examination, when he takes the words out of the context of this expert report and cross-examines by using such words taken out of the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we found that sentence. Would you please read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly, Mr. President, and I believe it's exactly what I said it represented it said a moment ago, but I'll read the entire sentence: "Immediately upon the escalation of the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina General Spegelj, as a chief inspector of the Croatian defence ministry -- let me stop there, Mr. President. If you go back to the transcript, what I said was: "The HV chief inspector asked the Croatian Minister of Defence, returning to the text, asked, on 7 April 1992, from the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, to form a group of 1.200 soldiers, mostly Muslims, from the area of the operational zone Rijeka, and send them to Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, again, sir, are those not your words or is this something -- another part of your report that you want to change?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my words, but I don't think you have interpreted them in this way. You have twisted the order a little bit. But there is a record, I believe, of what you've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I think the record will show, sir, that I read your report word for word. Did someone named Daidza become involved with the HV efforts in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Daidza's full name is Mate Sarlija, but apparently his real name is Nijaz Batlak. He was the commander of the 1st Brigade, volunteers of the Croatian army, also known as Krajl Tomislav. His unit, and I have to admit that in the military archives I haven't found a single word about that unit - his unit was in April, or between April and June, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that he was in the area of Capljina. I'm sure of that. And this unit is -- just a moment, please. It is a unit that, on the 27th of May, 1992, by the decision of the president of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, was integrated with the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the name of Bosnia and Herzegovinian Brigade Kralj Tomislav. After this it was disbanded and it split into two parts, because it had been composed of Croats and Muslims. Croats established the unit Ludvig Pavlovic. I do not have a copy of this document, but it was published by General Hasan Efendic, in 1998, in his book that I am quoting in my report. So that is very interesting, isn't it? There are a few documents of direct communication between Mr. Daidza and Mr. Izetbegovic regarding combat activities in the area of Konjic and Jablanica, where Daidza complained to Mr. Izetbegovic about a person who was called Zejnil Delalic, who apparently didn't obey him. You can find these documents in the state archives of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, your answer is yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a historian, and I cannot give you a simple yes or no. In this case there was a Daidza, and I told you exactly who he was, what he did, and how he ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you have to answer yes or no. Then you may explain why you answered that question. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not a single name was recorded in the transcript, and the witness mentioned his two names. The only thing that we have is Daidza. Can we have that repeated, and we also have a misspelling of Zejnil Delalic's name. I believe that this should enter the transcript. So maybe my learned friend would be kind enough and ask the witness to repeat all of the names under which Mr. Daidza was also known so that they can be recorded correctly in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that important?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I won't speak for Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you may repeat those names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Daidza, a general of the Croatian army, was also known as Mate Sarlija, but allegedly his real name is Nijaz Batlak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving on, sir, you say at page 11 of your report that "Due to the objections to the presence of the Croatian army in BH on the 7th of July, 1992, the deployment of the Croatian army outside the borders of the Republic of Croatia without the express order of the commander-in-chief was forbidden." It's my question to you about that part of your report was, whose objections? Who was objecting to the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe that it was primarily the international community who objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where were they in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time when they drew those objections?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanska Posavina. This mostly refers to that area, which was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that they would not -- the Croatian army units would not be allowed to be deployed outside the borders of Croatia without the express order of the commander-in-chief, who was the commander-in-chief that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the course of this trial - I know we're coming up on the break, Mr. President, but I think if we can get one or two more questions perhaps. In the course of this trial we've heard about a certain agreement between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic around the 21st of June, 1992, but if I understand your report, sir, again correctly, at page 11 your conclusion is that that agreement in fact did not change anything. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I would like to correct something first. We're talking about July, not June. And Mr. Izetbegovic's comment about this agreement you can find in my footnote -- in footnote 79. On that same evening, on the Croatian television, he -- I'm sorry. It's not 79. I apologise. I can't find it right now. But on the same evening he denies the military agreement, believing that such an agreement would be a threat to the Serbian people and that he is going to wait for the moves of the international community. And now I would like to take the opportunity to confirm a high degree -- a higher degree of the lack of cooperation on the part of the Muslims than the one that we talked about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The bottom line, sir, is that even though that agreement has been discussed in this courtroom, that agreement in fact never took affect, as you just told us, and didn't change anything, did it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say -- in the military aspect it didn't change anything. And as for the other aspects, I don't know. And in any case, this was not a military agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's 3.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I humbly ask this Chamber to ask my learned friend how much longer is this cross-examination going to take?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, well, I'd rather make the comments, my answer, outside the presence of the witness. If the witness could be excused or ....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, would you please take the witness out of the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's clear, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's become clear, Your Honour, by one of your interventions Mr. President, a few minutes ago the witness has apparently, as the court will observe, has become since yesterday increasingly aggressive and has set up on a course - it's rather obvious - to set up on a course to give long, non-responsive answers. Now, whenever I try to cut him off, interrupt, when I believe the question has been answered, as you did, yes or no, of course I draw an objection from the Defence. So I do not necessarily intend to intervene, and the witness can go on for ten minutes. He can give ten-minute non-responsive answers, if that's the way we wish to proceed. If that's the case, this cross-examination will indeed take a very long time, probably will not finish today. If the witness gives responsive answers and conducts himself properly, then it can be conducted, be finished much more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think in most cases in the cross-examination, the witnesses are rather hostile, at least to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case, to your positions. So try to - excuse me - try to organise your questions during the break and to see whether if we could save some time, you know, for the next sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With all respect, Mr. President, it's not the organisation of my questions. I expect the witness to be hostile to me. I quite expect that. That is not my -- he can be hostile all he wants and I certainly won't ask him to have any different feelings for me that he might have. That is not the issue. The issue is the giving of completely non-responsive answers, which take a long amount of time. Referring to footnotes and about topics that were not related to my questions at all. And that's what's taking time, Your Honour, with all respect, not the organisation of my questions. But I will certainly try to conclude it. But in answer to counsel's question, counsel asked you to ask me about the length of the cross-examination, and my answer is: It depends on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that you almost covered all the questions in this report. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because we came to page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, sir, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We have not talked about the extensive HVO presence and involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the spring of 1993 on. Right now we are at the end of 1992, and his report throughout goes on to talk about the extensive involvement, and our contention, in the case that we will put to the witness, extensive HV involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina, fighting against the Muslims throughout 1993, and that topic has not been covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that's the gist of this case and what we want to hear from this witness. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. You stand up first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't believe my ears. I don't believe that I've heard what my learned friend has said. And his comments upon his relationship with the witness, which legal system allows for that anywhere in the world? How many times you have warned us, Mr. President, that it is our fault if our relationship with the witness is not correct? You have repeated this a hundred times in this courtroom. And now you allow the Prosecutor to comment upon the witness's behaviour. The witness is such as he is because of his attitude towards him, and he is doing it on purpose. Why have we never had any problems with cross-examination conducted by Mr. Poriouvaev or Mr. Stringer? Why do we always have such problems when it is Mr. Scott who is in charge of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I completely second Mr. Krsnik, and I would like to add to that that if we are going to expect that the Prosecutor is going to receive the answer he expects and that he likes, then we can prolong this trial for another 14 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And still we haven't got the answer as to how long the cross-examination is going to take. We are still awaiting that answer. For how long does he intend to go on with his cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you have to understand that whenever there is a problem between the cross-examination and the witness, first we have to blame, if I may say that, to the cross-examiners in this respect. Because I understand, you know, some witnesses are not professional and they are not trained to give some evidence, especially with some professors, some lecturers, you know. They have the intention to give a very long statement, which might be out of the scope of the subject-matter in this case. We have to take a good lead, you know, in all the questionings. So having said that, we'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us in your report, and you discussed in the course of your testimony so far that there was fighting between the HVO and the Muslim armed forces around Prozor in October 1992, which you say on page 16 "finished with the utter defeat of the local ABiH units." Now, as I read your report, you agree that HV units, that is, units or elements of the army of Croatia, were involved in that fighting; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I quote Muslim authors who claim this. I did not find that anywhere, although the material about the Prozor conflict is more than voluminous, but that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's exactly the reason that we've gone through so much of your report in so much detail, for that very reason, that sometimes, respectfully, it's difficult to tell what your position is. So it's your position that the HV was not involved in the fighting around Prozor. Do I understand you now correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did not see the English translation, but I drew a clear distinction. I indicated where I was quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that the 113th HV Split Brigade and parts of the 114th Sibenik Brigade were not in fact engaged at Prozor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find any evidence of their participation, and therefore hold that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it also your position, then, that other elements of the 114th Sibenik Brigade and also the is 123rd Varazdin Brigade of the Croatian army were not engaged at that time around Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us clear up one thing here first. The 114th Sibenik Brigade does not exist, nor does the 123rd Varazdin Brigade. The 114th Brigade of the Croatian army comes from Split. The 123rd Brigade of the Croatian army comes from Slavonska Pozega. Regardless of the poor intelligence level of the BH army, which is obviously the source of all these untruths, nowhere have I found so far any evidence that these two units participated in the area of Prozor or the area of Travnik in 1992. That is as far as I know, this information was fabricated, was concocted for the first time, the institute for crime investigation in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the time that you say you were engaged as a soldier in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you familiar with the Colonel Zeljko Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name, not him personally. That is a man who was -- who at the time that we are talking about was the commander of the north-west Herzegovina operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he had been -- was at the time, was he not, an HV officer?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think he was ever an officer in the HV. But as far as I know, there was a fad at the time, which I think was started by General Praljak, and he was then conferred upon the status of an officer in the Croatian army, but I do not know exactly when. I think he was on the list of the 115th Brigade of the Croatian army in Imotski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not sure from your answer when you say he was on the list of the 115th Brigade, are you talking about Slobodan Praljak or are you talking about Mr. Siljeg?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about Mr. Siljeg. He was put there at the intervention of Mr. Praljak. He was made a member of the 115th Brigade, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could assist us by showing the witness Exhibit 186.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report to Mr. Siljeg, dated the 24th of October, 1992, and directing your attention to the first paragraph, it says: "Constant combat activity, the town of Prozor and Rama Lake are under the control of the Prozor HV/HVO."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we talk about the original, which is in Croatian? Nothing else. And let us have the witness read what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, has the witness been furnished with the original document? Witness, do you have the original document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, and I also have a copy which must have been coded before it was transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm sorry. Could we have the two documents compared, and also the document which is handwritten? I'd like to have the report that the Prosecutor is referring to the original which was -- which is handwritten and which is attached here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original is handwritten, and it says "HVO Prozor," but in the copy it says "HV Prozor." So obviously somebody made a mistake when copying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right, sir. That's your interpretation. And you do not agree, then --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I protest. It is not the interpretation; it is the original document, what it says. So the witness is not interpreting anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the original document that I have in the typed version says "HV." So that's why I'm saying -- I understand he's interpreting it, but that's what the original typed B/C/S version says. It says "HV."

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even that is not true, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, judging from the handwritten document, we only see "HVO Prozor," on the third line. We do not see "HV." Maybe there's a problem of translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No doubt about that, Your Honour, especially since there is a sign after "HV" which tells us that whoever copied it made a mistake. But this is a coded report. The handwritten -- which in its handwritten form is sent to the Croatian Defence Council, to the headquarters of the Croat Defence Council. The document -- the conflict is documented by a large number of documents. The Prosecutor, I'm quite sure, had access to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the -- around the same time, not exactly the 24th of October, I'm not suggesting, but in the fall of 1992, Jajce fell to Serb forces, which I think you've referred to several times at other places in your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jajce fell towards the end of October. I think it was the 29th or the 30th of October, which means six days after this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it your position also that elements of the Croatian army, the HV, were not involved in that fighting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us please clear up something. What do you mean by "element of the Croatian army"? And to avoid it in the future. That is, to understand what you mean when you ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Units, elements that are units, individual soldiers and officers, members of the Croatian army, sir. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very broad term, Mr. Prosecutor. If you do that, then you can call one man from some brigade, you can call him a brigade numbering several thousand men. An individual is an individual. As far as I know, I can name an officer of the Croatian army who was up there, Fikret Cuskic, the commander of the 1st Battalion -- of the first Krajina Battalion who, in May 1992, left from Velesajam from the fairground in Zagreb who became brigadier general of the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I guess there you could find a Croat here and there. Units, I mean units of the Croatian army, those I did not see. I must admit, though, that the material from Jajce is very meager and not much of it has been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Throughout, sir, the first part of 1993, moving from the end of 1992 into the first half of 1993, the Croatian army continued to give close support to the HVO in Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it continued to give logistical support, and I think it did it for yet another army in that area until mid-April. But that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask that the witness be shown Exhibit 746.01 and 262.01. Would you please give the witness both of those at the same time, to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Taking them chronologically, sir, if you look first at 746.01, you indicated earlier today that Mr. Marinovic was the commander of the southern front in 1993. This appears to be a report from Mr. Marinovic dated the 8th of February, 1993, reporting on an inspection of HVO forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that common practice, for the HV to give support, to inspect, and then assist HVO forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the first half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a link between the command of the south east Herzegovina operative zone and Croatian army units from -- well, this is obviously sector south, meaning the southern front, and this is the inspection control of the link towards the Herzegovina corps of the army of Republika Srpska. I think this was the regular practice on the southern front at this link.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I could ask you to look at 262.01. This is a report from, so the record is clear, again from Mr. Marinovic, the command of sector south, to, among others, chief of staff of the Croatian army, Janko Bobetko again about the plan of engagement I'm looking at the first introductory paragraph under the addressee section on the basis of demonstrated need and the order of the chief of the Main Staff of the HV and according to the plan of engagement of the commander of sector south. Another HVO unit inspected and supported by the HV; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said, and so let me clarify it once again. The link between the HVO and HV in this area was, with these two brigades only. The first Brigade from Capljina and the 4th HVO Brigade, this is March, so it came from three municipalities, and the front line was in the eastern part of Herzegovina, and I think this was the regular practice of the Croatian army, to visit the troops and carry out inspection because of the position of Dubrovnik. It was important to include the positions of these units in the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these units, these HVO units, were actively involved with the 115th HV Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into 1993 at the southern front, but I think that with these two brigades of the HVO, there were also three Croatian army brigades engaged. Well, 115, as likely as not -- if you have it somewhere. I didn't read the document. And there should have been, I presume, 116th from Metkovic, and of course the 163rd -- 163rd Brigade of the Croatian army from Dubrovnik, and from time to time, from the area of Zagreb, individual battalions from Zagreb brigades came to reinforce the troops in that area, both reserve and guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, both at the time when the Serbs -- excuse me - the Croats and Muslims together were fighting the Serbs, and later, when the Croats were fighting against the Muslims, military support flowed from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina in very large amounts; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military support flowed, no doubt. The size of it, I wouldn't know. HV logistics documents were accessible to me only in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that support, sir, continued into the time during -- when the HVO was fighting against the Muslims; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the very inception of the HVO until the end of the war, that is, from April 1992 until, say, late autumn 1995, the Croatian army provided logistical support to the Croat defence council. I believe I've said somewhere that this same applied to Muslims, with the break in the support during their conflict, during the war of the Muslims against the Croats, that is, for about a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In addition to material support, sir, isn't it true that a very large percentage of the HVO officer corps either had been or were at the time of their service in Bosnia-Herzegovina HV officers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small percentage of officers, not large, as you are claiming. I doubt that there were ever more than 100, 100 men in the HVO. That is, I do not think that more than 100, 150 men, members of the HVO, came from the Croatian army. After Prozor, which is interesting, in the agreement between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic, where Mr. Praljak was appointed a member of the joint command, I do not understand what you are trying to say with this, except perhaps that Mr. Izetbegovic -- that Mr. Izetbegovic's term of office had expired, during which he was a lawful president, so this could only be the signature of the president of the Party of Democratic Action, and you can bat your eyes as much as you like. I'd merely like to quote to you something from an officer of the BH army referring to this. This is footnote 104, please. This was noted in his diary by Mirsad Catic, an officer in the BH army, commander of the technical group 1, on the 13th of November, 1992. I quote: "Jagonjac and Praljak are in some joint staff which is to be in place of the Supreme Command in Sarajevo. What will this bring about, who to obey. Divjak and Karic are confused." General Divjak at that moment is an ornament in the joint staff, and Mr. Karic, Mr. Karic, is one of the high-ranking officers, high-ranking officers of the BH army. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we understand what you are going to say. Mr. Scott, your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you talk about 100 to 150 persons, my question to you specifically was about officers, senior officers in the HVO, many of them were senior HV officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that all of these individuals were high-ranking officers of the HV. Some of them were high-ranking officers in the Croatian army, specifically the highest-ranking ones were the already mentioned General Praljak, General Roso. I think that sometime in the beginning, that is, in April or May, for a short while a brigadier Gotovina, he was a brigadier then, brigadier Crnjac, made quick appearances, but they were at the level of brigades. There were some officers, especially towards the end of 1993, in the Croat defence council who had the brigadier level in the Croatian army. So they should -- they ought to be high-ranking officers. But there are not as many of them as you are claiming. And then I think that from that period there is a circular letter sent to all brigades which allows to establish the exact number of all the levels. I'm surprised that you don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, certain questions that you do not ask this witness again and again. I think the question you asked has no fundamental difference with the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reason I asked it a second time, Your Honour, was because it wasn't answered the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, he answered this question. It's quite clear to us they are officers. There are 100 to 150 officers. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that included, did it not, sir, Milivoj Petkovic, who at one time was the head of the HVO for a substantial period of time? He was a senior HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have forgotten him. I believe that he was there before the HVO came. I think that he was the head of the mortars, artillery, in the Split operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the witness to be shown at the same time, please, Exhibits P121.2 and 786.01. It should be in the second -- what was the second bundle originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that Exhibit 121.2 is a time indicating that Mr. Petkovic, Colonel Petkovic, at the time had allegedly left the HV army, and on Exhibit 786.01 is when he returned to the HV army, to the HV? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And during a period of time, he was the head of the entire HVO army, was he not, before Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was effectively, from April 1992 until September 1994, except for the period between July 1993 and, I believe, March or April 1994, was the first soldier of the HVO. But he remained the chief of the Main Staff, and during that time the function of the commander of the HVO was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown Exhibits 134.11 and 359.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exhibit 134.11, sir, is an order from the Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak, dated the 5th of June, 1992, sending 13 soldiers to the southern front. Among those, you may notice Miro Andric, Blaz Andric, Branko Kozul, Mirsad Sivac. And if I could direct your attention, please, to Exhibit 359.2, all those men listed here as part of the 101st HV Brigade, these officers, were still in Bosnia in May 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Colonel Andric, at the time of the second report, was a member of the joint command of the army of the HV and the BH army -- HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the BH army. And I've had the opportunity to see this document, and what you're trying to say is probably that some of the officers' term of service stopped, and for some of them it continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The man Zeljko Akrap, which is mentioned in Defence Exhibit D2/77, he was another of these HV officers serving in the HVO, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The case is the same as with Mr. Andric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, sir, both in your testimony on Tuesday and in your report, I put to you that you have been careful in the selection of the words you've used to describe these, the status of many of the HV soldiers or officers, and I'll refer you to page 18, at least in the English version. I'll give you a footnote. Page 18 of your report. It's before -- it's right after Exhibit -- excuse me - footnote 151. You say: "Which were in documents mostly recorded as volunteers." And in your testimony on Tuesday, sir, you said: "They were regarded as volunteers." My question to you, sir: Were they -- it's not whether they were recorded or regarded as volunteers, but were they in fact volunteers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would adhere to what I have written in here. The only unit that we can discuss and talk about, whether it was a volunteers' unit, is the 5th Guards Brigade. From the 5th or 6th July 1993, it was down there in Herzegovina. Later on it moved to the area of Prozor and Gornji Vakuf. And that unit, with a short interruption, had the strength of one infantry battalion, and this may raise an issue of the number of the volunteers. As for the others, the 1st and the 2nd Guards Brigade are volunteer brigades. I was in the war with some of their men. And reserve brigades could not be sent if the members didn't want to go. They were usually very small, except for one battalion from Slavonia which was composed of the 5th Guards Brigade and the 127th Brigade of the Croatian army. Obviously, I would like to draw your attention to the 175th Brigade. That brigade was mobilised and composed of deserters and was sent down there to the area of Prozor i.e., it was never complete as one battalion. Its corps was undoubtedly volunteer, but the officer corps were volunteers, whereas its men were mobilised on the request of the president of the HZ HB sometime in October 1993 or maybe in September of that same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mobilised by whom, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mobilised by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, like they mobilised in 1992 for the purposes of the BH army. I believe that there is an agreement on the return of conscripts to their respective states.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, they may have been volunteers in one sense, they may have volunteered to go to Bosnia, but they were, and continued to be, HV soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They retained -- if you are referring to the members of the HV, they have retained the rights of the members of the Croatian army, which was customary after the request of Mr. Spegelj dating back to the 7th April 1992. So both Croats and Muslims who went down there had the right to retain the status of members of the Croatian army upon their return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, one example of that in Exhibit P122.1 specifically says: "All who go retain all the rights of HV soldiers, including monthly salaries," correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the question -- saying, using the terminology "volunteers," isn't it correct, sir, doesn't get us very far in this sense, if the Croatian Minister of Defence Jozo Susak says: "I want a brigade of volunteers to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a brigade of people volunteer, they're still -- it's still the HV, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We again arrive at the same thing. It is not Susak who wants a brigade. It is Spegelj who wants a brigade of Muslims for the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that brigade was indeed sent down there. It was the 7th Krajina Brigade, which later on was incorporated in the BH army. And I really don't know when and how many stopped their status in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, these were not volunteers in the sense of being independent of an organised HV effort at all, were they? These weren't just individuals who just happened to go to Bosnia; they were part of the Croatian army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They retained the status of the Croatian army, but I don't have any proof, and I don't believe you do either, to show that the Croatian army retained control over them when they moved into Bosnia and Herzegovina. Maybe you should be a bit more cautious when you put forth such allegations. I really haven't seen this. I'm sure that you must have had more time to inspect the documents in the state archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I've patiently waited for both the question and the answer, and I would like to draw your attention to the fact that despite your previous warning, the Prosecutor repeats himself. One answer is given, and then the question is repeated again.
