So that really means that we are going to be here for another 14 months in order for the Prosecutor to finally get the answer that he really wants to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we understand where are you leading to. We quite understand. I think we have already get what we want in this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it correct that all these, and if we need to go to the transcripts, presidential transcripts, we will, that these people sent as "volunteers" were sent by President Tudjman as the commander-in-chief by Susak as the Minister of Defence, even knowing that they would call them volunteers but they were being sent as an organised effort by the Republic of Croatia? Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I think the witness answered that when he said that there's no evidence that after these volunteers who retained rights went to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that they remained under the control of the army. So logically, the next step for you to take would be to put that piece of evidence in rebuttal or move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would be happy to move to the next piece of evidence, and that would be, then, presidential transcript 13, PT13. If that could be shown to the witness, please. You may wish to show him PT14 at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I can direct your attention to -- if you again, please, use for reference the numbers on the upper left corner - excuse me - upper right corner of the Croatian-language part of the exhibit that's been given to you, and if you look for the numbers R 0156977, beginning toward the bottom of that page in the conversation or statements attributed to the president, and for the English readers, page 1 of Exhibit PT13. You say there was no evidence of this. Let me put this to you. Starting at the words "right until now, in June, I called the minister and the chief of headquarters, and at the beginning of July I asked, I told them, in Bosnia-Herzegovina war is now being waged for the area of the border of the Croatian state. Accordingly, one has to do everything to help this area to hold out. It is not the same to us whether the border of the Croatian state, that is, will be Jajce, with Travnik and only with Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca. In diplomatic talks we have not given up on Kiseljak and Kresevo, but we have agreed that this is in so we might achieve this to, so that the Muslim state at the request of Europe should have the conditions for territorial existence. We, that is, have given up on Kresevo, that is, agreed that Kresevo and Kiseljak should be in the Muslim state. It was kind of a situation since war is being waged, we don't know when they took Vares, but Kiseljak has become important to us, so that we can link up with Busovaca and with a whole entire territory here," it says. Now the next paragraph: "We had to do all this, of course, under the cover of sending volunteers, but gentlemen from the ministry and the minister and the chief of the main headquarters, people say correctly that when we brought they did not get this help from Croatia in time." Skipping down a couple of paragraphs: "So it is the task, your task, of all you who are here, for us to hear what you have undertaken and what forces to send there to make sure, materially and in personnel, that we defend these areas. The borders of Croatia plus these -- this here, we have an agreement with Fikret Abdic if the union does not endure, that then this joins Croatia, that is, the borders of the Croatian state are like this, and clearly with this." They were sent, organised, and directed by Republic of Croatian government; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is authentic, then you are close enough. Your allegation does seem to be pretty correct. But there is something further on in the text, and if I may, I would like to read it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under the Rules, sir, I suppose you can say or read anything that you want.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a sentence on page 4, or R 0156980, the last passage: "Therefore, please find people who will go, because they are not needed in the Croatian state, in the Croatian army. A hundred pilots or I don't know what, and they tell me there are no pilots there who would fly to bring here where the destiny of the Croatian state is being resolved for the future." Now I would like to comment upon this, if I may. This is a good document in favour of the Prosecution; however, we are still talking about very few members of the Croatian army in that area. In my footnote 150, I gave you a heap of documents where you can -- in which you can see what their number really was. And regardless of this very interesting transcript that I would be very grateful to receive from you a copy of, still there were very few men down there, according to my estimate, their number never exceeded a light brigade, which then raises the question of these efforts, as you call them; i.e., it was not possible to carry out any such effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going to go through every presidential transcript, I can assure the Chamber, at this time. Sir, are you suggesting that this same Republic of Croatia that was fighting against the Serbs to establish the future borders of the Croatian state, and by your own admission, they were there extensively in 1992, that the Republic of Croatia was willing to stand by and lose the war to the Muslims in 1993? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to say that this is the way you interpret things. But I would like to offer a different kind of interpretation. This is -- this was the war for territories, which was launched in April by the BH army, and that the Croatian army symbolically on the ground, that is, members of the Croatian army, helped to maintain the Croatian Defence Council, and what was the character of the attack of the BH army is illustrated by my footnote 152. Rasim Delic, the chief of the Main Staff, i.e., the chief of the Main Staff of the BH army, at the beginning of 1994, in front of the congress of Bosnian intellectuals, said, amongst other things, that the HVO was defeated militarily, and thus the concept of the Croatian community Herceg-Bosna, which had only survived the engagement of very significant forces of the army of the Republic of Croatia, otherwise they would have completely vanished from these territories, vanished both as a political and a military force. As I said, the Croatian forces were meager, and General Delic forgot to say one thing here, they would have disappeared as an ethnic group. So this is the right that we were talking about yesterday and that the right for suspension. And you can find the confirmation in every place that the BH army, as they say, liberated from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber has evidence that Slobodan Praljak, on the 14th of March, 1992, was appointed as an assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Did he stop being an assistant Minister of Defence during the time that he was the chief of the HVO in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During that period, I believe he wasn't an assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you base that on?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he returned to the HV, he was appointed an advisor to the minister in charge of the military archive. And I also believe that I saw an order on his discharge dating back to July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just to follow up on Judge Clark's guidance, I'm just trying to mark which exhibits we will perhaps simply save for rebuttal, not to prolong this any longer than necessary. Could the witness please be shown Exhibits 562.12 -- 562.12, and 559.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, starting with 562.12, it appears to be a communication by Brigadier Zarko Tole, described in the document as chief of the HVO Main Staff, addressed to the president of the Republic of Croatia personally, to the defence minister of the Republic of Croatia personally, dated the 9th of August, 1993, talking about a meeting with the head of the Croatian army, General Janko Bobetko, and the commander of the southern front, who you've identified for us today, Mr. Marinovic, requesting a number of items in support of the HVO, including tanks, to send the 1st Battalion of the 5th Guards Brigade. Is that correct, sir? Is that consistent with your findings of the HV involvement in the Mostar region in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document refers to Gornji Vakuf, and indeed sometime in August there appeared a Tactical Group. I believe this is what they called it - of the 5th Guards Brigade, composed of a complete brigade. So it was not a battalion in the establishment sense, but I believe that the strength of that unit was an incomplete infantry battalion, some 600 men altogether. And this is interesting to provide comment upon your previous documents about Mr. Marinovic. This shows you how forces were pulled out from the southern front, the wing, or the link, where you tried -- purported to put the HVO under the complete control of the HV. I believe that this enclosure that is mentioned of the corporeal of the 5th Brigade would clarify things much better. But in any case, in August of 1993, I mentioned that in one of my footnotes, gives you the strength of the 5th Guards Brigade in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the last part of the communication for Mr. Tole, he says: "Following a conversation with the commander of the 5th Guards Brigade, Brigadier Kapular, we're setting forth his proposal and submitting it to you as a special attachment." Now, sir, if you'll direct your attention to Exhibit 559.1, it appears to be a request from Slobodan Praljak to the Ministry of Defence to Gojko Susak. We ask you to place HV officers brigadier Zarko Tole and brigadier Ivan Kapular, at the disposal of the HVO General Staff." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see it from this request. Except that I'd like to correct you. This is Stanko Matic's signature, and he's one of the assistants to the command -- to the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO. But I'd like to comment, to make a comment. We come to what I said in my report, after all, and what I said that between October 1992 to July 1993, there are no members or larger groups -- by larger groups, we mean platoons of the Croatian army, and there are none of them in the territory of Herceg-Bosna. It only happens other events in Mostar, that is, following the 30th of June, 1993, when an HVO unit with Muslim members betrayed the unit and crossed over to the BH army side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll resume at a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've significantly shortened the remaining exhibits for these purposes, but I'm afraid you'll see an expanded bundle for rebuttal purposes. But we'll try to finish in the next few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: What do you mean by "next few minutes"?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I hope in 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you were talking before the break about the 7th Guards Brigade and in your report you say this was the second-most-involved HV unit in Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professional, the second in terms of its strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall where it was that they were engaged, 7th Guards?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can follow from sometime in November, that is, October/November 1993, one can see them in the area of Gornji Vakuf, but their strength not going beyond an incomplete company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to please provide the witness with the following four exhibits, which I think will be the last exhibits that we'll use: 712.3, 745.3, 780.2, and 842.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, to look first at 712.3, a communication from Zeljko Siljeg, commander of the operation zone, on the 13th of December, 1993, and if I could ask you to look at, please, section headed "Capital D," D as in dog. Do you see where it says "we would like you to see the decision or solution for a part of the forces of the 7th Guards Brigade, Branko Predragovic claims that Dragovic had received an order from General Janko Bobetko that prior to 15 December the unit should withdraw from Skopje, which should be the Skopje or - I'm not going to try to pronounce that version, excuse me - battlefield. My question to you, sir: Would this document be consistent with the 7th Guards Brigade was in the area of Gornji Vakuf in late 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That agrees with what I said, that a company of the 7th Guards Brigade was in the area at the indicated time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall, by the way, the name of the 7th Guards Brigade, what they went by?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, it was called PUMA. That was its war name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in your report, you also mention the HV 1st Guards Brigade. Was the 1st Guards Brigade known as the Tigrovi, or Tigers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also mentioned the 2nd HVO Guards Brigade, and was their name the Gromovi, or Thunder?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you said that the 7th Guards Brigade was the second most extensively involved HV unit in Herzegovina at that time. What was the first -- that was the second. What was the first most extensively involved HV unit?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. The 5th Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the name of that unit, other than "5th Guards" in the sense of PUMA of Gromovi, what was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sokol, Pokum [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, that many of these professional units, both HV units and, for that matter, HVO units, received their salaries through the Croatian army in late 1993 and continuing into early 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- personally, I don't think I really saw many documents about that, but this is a widespread claim, and I do not think it is brought into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me show you one specific instance, then. If you could look at Exhibit 745.3. This is a correspondence from a man named Dragan Curcic, the commander of the Ludvig Pavlovic unit to the commander of the southern front, as you've identified him earlier, Mr. Marinovic, dated the 5th of February, 1994. And does not Mr. -- or Colonel Curcic request the payment of war allowances for our unit from the southern front?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this letter, it seems beyond doubt. But let me say something concerning the Ludvig Pavlovic Battalion. As I've already said, Ludvig Pavlovic emerged in June 1992, and it was an offspring of the Kralj Tomislav, that is former Daidza's regiment, when it split into its Croat and its Muslim part. Some of those men had contracts signed with the Croatian army, so that part of the men -- some men of this unit were paid by Croatia, that is, received -- and others were getting much lower salaries, because they only had their contracts with the HVO. I know, because that unit shared the barracks with my 1st Guards Brigade in Capljina. Dragan Curcic, they only had its army post in Vrgorac. Otherwise it was an exclusive HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In fact, sir, for all practical purposes, both financially and otherwise, in terms of the make-up of the unit, wasn't the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade an HV unit throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, as far as I know, never received any orders -- no. Let's first explain this. This is a battalion, and an incomplete guards battalion. When Bobetko left the southern front, I never saw an HV's order issued to that unit, and it was under no obligation to us, that is, the military archive of the Ministry of Defence of Croatia, to turn over the material, so that I think - I repeat - I haven't seen a single document, any proof to corroborate your claim. Later on it became part of the 2nd Guards Brigade of the HVO. That is, it simply vanished as a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "a battalion," this was a battalion of a guards brigade, how large a unit at that time was a battalion? How many soldiers and officers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A professional battalion of the Croatian army and the HVO numbers 760 men, but the formations varied in size. I think that in 1994 to 1995, Ludvig Pavlovic numbered some 350 men. I know that the Bruno Busic regiment was to have 2.000, it had 60 [as interpreted]. But in real life it had 620 men. I don't know as far as the Convicts Battalion is concerned. I think that Vitezovi, the 9th, might have been a hundred men strong. And as for the Croatian army, professional battalions also varied in size from perhaps 15, the 8th light assault, to perhaps 200 in the 7th Guards. So that the term "battalion" needs to be treated with caution, and one should try to establish the actual strength. And as for the Croatian army at the time that we are talking about, that is, members of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think that documents allow not only to glean the strength but also every individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you mentioned the Convicts Battalion in this context because it was considered a professional unit?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I quoted somewhere a document from early 1993. This is a covert -- a big report which considers it a professional unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, would you agree with me that the fighting that was going on in the second half of 1993 between the Croats and Muslims, we're not talking about large NATO-type armies fighting each other, were we, in terms of quality of equipment, in terms of size of units, in terms of professional forces? Correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't understand this question somehow. Could you perhaps clarify it in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask the question differently. In the circumstances, and given the nature of the fighting that was taking place in the area at the time, would you agree with me, sir, that even a unit of between 300 to 600 professional soldiers, well-equipped and disciplined soldiers, could make a significant difference on the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't really agree with your claim, but I think it suffices to analyse their war career in Bosnia during that period of time. And I believe that yesterday or the day before yesterday I already said that these units were mostly engaged around villages, that is, at features, or to simplify, hills. And I can give an example of the 5th Guards. In the latter half of 1993, it was on the Gornji Vakuf front, and of nine sectors of that front line, it held one sector, and the other, the remaining sectors, were held by the HVO. And more often than not, these units were used for the defence. And as I personally witnessed the arrival of even such small units meant significant psychological support to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it true, sir, that also during the war, and even after the war in the terms of the war in terms of the Bosnian Croat war, even in early 1994, mid-1994, that many HVO officers, if they had not already been HV officers, became HV officers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me show you, just as one example, Exhibit 780.2. This is an appointment by President Franjo Tudjman of an officer named Predrag Mandic, from Siroki Brijeg, to the rank of colonel in the HV army. Did you ever know a Mr. Mandic during any of your tours of duty in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard of Mr. Mandic. He was in Bosnia. But as far as I know, he was only a member of the HVO. But basically, this is what I've already told you regarding Zeljko Siljeg, that some HVO officer -- for some HV officers, it was a question of status or social prestige to be an officer in the Croatian army, and so this is how they acquired this status of officers in the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, sir, I asked you on -- I asked you yesterday if, because of your involvement with the archives in Zagreb you are aware of the fact that -- or I put the question to you about the taking of the -- many of the HVO documents to Croatia for the purposes of concealing or keeping them from international investigators. And sir, if I can direct your attention to Exhibit 842.1. And if you can find -- in the English version it is page 23; in the Croatian version, sir, if you could find the heading -- the section VI, or the English, if you can read it, which, in the course of your testimony, it appears that you can read a fair amount of English. Whichever is easiest for you. Who was, by the way, Markica Rebic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markica Rebic, as you can see from this, was assistant minister for security affairs of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did not Mr. Rebic, indicated here as a deputy minister, write to President Franjo Tudjman, on the 4th of June, 1998, and reporting on the activities of his organisation: "When HVO archives became a serious problem in the course of preparation of General Blaskic's defence with respect to the substance of the subpoena, and ICTY's request involving HVO officials, this service, in cooperation with the HIS, took action and measures to protect the HVO archives."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I truly do not know what is the relevance of this, in the light of the indictment of my client and generally. We heard today very many irrelevant things, but this now I do not want to gloss over this. How is this document relevant to the indictment? I repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that yesterday this question was brought up, and this witness has been working here for quite a considerable time. The Prosecution asked the question yesterday, and today he showed him a document if he knows or has reason to know such things happened. That's quite logical. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, except that I couldn't find. That allegedly is not important. Yesterday I said clearly that I was engaged in putting this material into order. I do not know who, how, when, and why brought, or rather, transferred this material. All I did was to put this material in a shape which allows it to be used. I had no hand in anything else concerning this material. So my task was strictly professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my final question to you is this: You told us you worked for three different directors of the Croatian intelligence service HIS, the second being Miroslav Tudjman, the third one being Ozren Zunec, and during that time, sir, and your work with these documents, you never learned and you were never told that in fact these documents had been taken out of Bosnia-Herzegovina to keep them from subpoenas and requests coming from this Tribunal; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first I'd say -- I'd put it as follows: My task was unambiguous and I was assigned to this task -- I started doing it reluctantly only when I was told that would be removed from the military archive for two months. And after I saw how things stood, I said this was two years' worth of work. And then, as I have said, and you repeat it now, there were three different directors who were protagonists of different political options and that at that time in the Croatian press there was on a rampage something that was called intelligence work, and I think that I didn't use the name, but nevertheless I was -- my name -- I figured in the press as some kind of a collaborator of Markica Rebic's who was destroying the material, the records down there. And after all that, I really felt quite uninclined, disinclined to talk with anyone, and I do not think anyone tried to talk to me. I was assigned to do something, and I believe I did it very well. I wasn't even asked to write a single report. Which also speaks about the nature of my work. This was a hot potato, which everybody ignored, and it was my task to put it in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on your answer, one follow-up question, then: Which documents or what documents were marked -- was Markica Rebic destroying, as you just said on line 16?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that the press, and more specifically, Nacional, which is a weekly, claimed that while I was there, nothing was destroyed. I don't know whether some things like that happened later on. Later on, all this was transferred into the state archives, and I doubt that anything was destroyed. These were the so-called intelligence wars within the Croatian intelligence community, and I was a scapegoat, and I was named not by name, although some later tried to explain that this referred to somebody else whose name I saw in this document that is dated 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marijan, my questions will follow up on the questions asked by my learned friend Scott. Did Muslims want an independent state of Croatia with a border on the Drina during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning, it was a very strong movement in 1941, and then in 1942, 1943 there appeared a stream of autonomous, which tried to create some sort of a Muslim state. I must admit, I am not clear on the borders within which they wanted to have that state. And they tried to do that by sending letters to Benito Mussolini the Italian dictator, and to Adolf Hitler, the German dictator.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did Muslims, and to what extent, belong to the Ustasha movement?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to some estimates, every fourth member of the army of the independent state of Croatia, both Ustasha as well as the Home Guards, were of Muslim ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What side was Franjo Tudjman on?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Tudjman was a partisan. He belonged to the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, i.e., to its military wings, also known as partisans, the adequate English term for that would be the guerrilla.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: From the historical sources that you have collected, can you tell us what was the strength of the BH army in late 1992 or in spring 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say, and I've already said that the commander of the 3rd Corps, when talking to the representatives of the HVO, he bragged that he had 40.000 men, which means, if this was true, that only the 3rd Corps, which was deployed in the area of Central Bosnia, that it was more numerous than the entire HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What can a unit consisting of a thousand men do against such a force?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could maintain two neighbouring villages and a few elevations between them. A brigade has about 4.500 men. This is the norm. And it can defend a line of nine kilometres. And if the region is mountainous, then it can hold up to 12 kilometres of the line. And in the attack actions, this is halved, which means up to six. The HVO and the HV units, especially the professional units of the HV, mostly had less than 2.000 men, except for maybe the 5th Guards, which had somewhat over 2.000 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, did you work on collecting and analysing documents relative to the aggression of the Yugoslav People's Army and Yugoslavia against Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Has that material been given to the Prosecutor's office here in The Hague for the case against Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was, some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Scott or any other Prosecutor contact you with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have been contacted by the Prosecution, but not Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In those contacts, did somebody belittle you as a professional, as an expert, and deny your qualities, as this has been done in the past two or three days?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have been able to dispel some of their prejudices about Mr. Milosevic and I've been able to pinpoint some of the shortcomings and the failures that their teams have been -- have done when they were studying the role of Milosevic in the war against Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, have you ever been compensated by this Court for this expert study?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that this was under way?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I hear it now from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And now my last question. Is it your opinion, Mr. Marijan, that Yugoslavia was a historical anachronism?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an historical failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And to your mind, is Bosnia-Herzegovina an artificial concoction?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marijan, I will be very brief. I would like to clarify some things that you either were not able to express properly or you were interrupted in the middle of your explanations. I'm afraid that a lot of things have not been explained thoroughly here.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to write a book about this, you can rest assured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That would be a very good idea. I've been writing one myself. Mr. Marijan, kindly tell the Chamber: Are you familiar with the Dayton Accords and the Washington Accords?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in broad lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that the Washington Agreement has recognised all the laws of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna and that the same was done by the Dayton Accords and that these laws are applied to this very day in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, in the entity where Muslims and Croats live together?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the Washington agreement envisages the possibilities of a confederation of that same federation with the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is re-examination and not leading questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe that your question is out of the scope of the cross-examination. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, kindly repeat whether the Washington Agreement envisages any sort of confederation with the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a confederation of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina has been envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I know that you are not accustomed to the workings of a court, so some of the names that you have mentioned, people are not familiar with the ethnic background of some of the names as we are. You have mentioned an officer of the Croatian army by the name of Fikret Cuskic who was engaged in the area of Jajce. Can you please tell us what was his ethnic background and what was his lot?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fikret Cuskic is a Muslim by ethnic origin, a good soldier. He was a Captain First Class of the Yugoslav army in Varazdin. Then he moved and joined the Croatian army. He was an officer of the 1st mechanised Brigade of the Croatian army and then the commander of the 1st Krajina Battalion, and then, after the fall of Jajce, he was the commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade of the BH army, which is regarded as the best unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in very short lines: Was that a common occurrence in 1992 and in 1993, and what do you know about the arrival of the volunteers from the former socialist Republic of Bosnia, and later on only Bosnia, in -- that is, Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1992, so when the volunteers came and joined the war in the Republic of Croatia and their return when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started? Do you know anything about that? Did you study that phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about 1991 and Croatia and then return in 1992 to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't study that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my last question: I would like you to be shown the Exhibit IAC-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there are some clarifications needed here, and I'm going to ask you some questions about this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Please tell us: Where and when did you first see this document, and what do you think about its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I saw this document for the first time in the book --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. Before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I object to the question, Your Honour. What is the basis for this witness to express a view on the authenticity of a document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you might ask your question in another way, because we have heard that this witness has some views about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exactly what I wanted to hear from this witness, his views on this document. When my learned friend was examining him, he was not allowed to express freely his views of this document, and this is what I want to hear from the witness: What are his views of this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I saw this document twice. Both times in the books by Muslim authors, and I said that the first part underneath the conclusions is very strange but that this is a document that -- and that the agreements with Franjo Tudjman that are mentioned here, that there must be the minutes of these agreements that would then confirm whether this is a forgery or whether this is an authentic document. I don't have these minutes. Mr. Prosecutor may have them. I personally, I will probably know in a month or two whether this is authentic, because I have submitted a request for the insight into the transcripts of the president of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Witness, for coming here to give your evidence. Frankly speaking, I learned a lot from your report and from your testimony. Madam Usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home and your success in your future research.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, at this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. These are the documents that we discussed during the direct examination, and I have already dictated their numbers for the transcript, and so these are the documents: D259 to D278, that I'm tendering for admission. And obviously, the expert report by this witness, which is D2/79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections from the Prosecution side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. These documents are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, kindly, just a technical matter. I heard from our interpreters that our translation may have some ambiguities, and Judge Clark rightly asked me who translated it. So I would kindly ask you to allow us to again translate this document via the translators service of this Court, to make this translation more accurate than the one that we have now. I know that it may take some time, but it would assist us greatly, and I am asking for your indulgence in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your request is granted. We'll send it to the translation section and have it translated into proper English. Yes, Mr. Scott. At this stage, do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as the Court may have observed, since there was a selection process going on during the direct examination, I would be most appreciative if we could submit the selected documents in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please submit that request early next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So next Monday we'll sit in the afternoon and hear the last witness in Mr. Naletilic's case, another expert of history. Am I right, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to send you a confidential submission for your eyes only, and now I would not be prepared to answer that question, for the reasons of confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I hope I could read it tomorrow, so that we could arrange the hearings for the next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to pry into something confidential, but on the other hand, I don't think it's fair. It sounds -- I can only infer, of course, but it sounds to me that there may be some question about this witness in the schedule, and to be perfectly transparent, I'm not anxious for either myself or my staff to work the next three days for a witness who doesn't appear, and I mean that quite -- the next three days, between now and Sunday, or Monday morning, if he's not going to be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, would you please indicate in which area these filings will --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't know -- I'm trying to learn English, and because I see how important that is. Are we in two different courtrooms? I'm not -- I was not talking about the witness who should appear on Monday. He will be here. He will testify. And I just referred to the previous witness. I am preparing a submission that is very confidential, and you are going to receive it next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may file it in ex parte motions for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But not confidential --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Sorry. It's wrong word. Ex parte, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I'm confused now. Because are we talking about a confidential, a non-public filing served on counsel? Are we talking about an ex parte filing not served on counsel? Because in the transcript just now, it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an ex parte submission. My learned friend --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. President, concerning a witness who has already testified, I object to that. How are we to know to respond to something said secret about a witness who has already testified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since it's an ex parte filing and supposed to be confidential, we are in no position concerning with the contents of that filings. We'll make our decision when we receive it. Of course, in the meantime we'll bear in mind the interests of the Prosecution in this matter. Having said that, we'll resume next Monday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
